newsitem.title: USA: SOFT-SPOKEN HERMAN TROUBLESHOOTS UPS STRIKE.
newsitem.headline: SOFT-SPOKEN HERMAN TROUBLESHOOTS UPS STRIKE.

text.p: In the increasingly strident dispute between the Teamsters union and United Parcel Service, the role of peacemaker has fallen to President Clinton's petite, soft-spoken Labor secretary, Alexis Herman.

The 49-year-old African-American, who overcame race and sex barriers to win a coveted White House job and survived efforts to hold her Cabinet nomination hostage, hopes to breach the bitter chasm dividing the two sides in the year's biggest labor dispute.

"Alexis has had a history of people underestimating her," Joan Baggett, a labor official and former White House political director, told Business Week magazine recently. "She has a light touch, but she is very thorough."

Almost alone among the major players in the 10-day-old strike that has crippled the nation's major package carrier, Herman has remained quietly optimistic that the intractability of both sides will give way to renewed negotiations.
While UPS talks of an impasse and the Teamsters accuse the company of intimidation and greed, Herman wraps her public remarks in the gentler tones of a facilitator.
"I'm encouraged in that I believe both sides expressed a willingness to be more flexible in looking at their own differences," she said on Tuesday.

Herman has been an inside player in Washington for many years. During the administration of President Jimmy Carter she set up and ran training programs in the South and headed the Labor Department's Women's Bureau.

Before Clinton was elected, she served on the Democratic National Committee where she worked closely with the late Commerce Secretary Ron Brown. She was chief executive officer of the 1992 Democratic Convention and she worked with the president on his transition team.
Most recently, Herman served as director of White House public liaison.
Her nomination to the Labor post was a battle right from the start. Three powerful interest groups within the Democratic Party each pushed their favorite candidate.
Labor unions wanted former Pennsylvania Sen. Harris Wofford to get the job, Hispanics lobbied for Rep. Estaban Torres of California.

But Herman, strongly backed by the National Organization for Women and civil rights leader Jesse Jackson -- for whom she worked during the 1988 presidential campaign -- won the day, only to have her nomination deadlocked for months by partisan political wrangling in the Senate.

Although Herman may not have been labor's candidate for the post, they soon rallied around the new secretary, noting her close relationship with Clinton and familiarity with internal White House politics as considerable pluses.
"Alexis Herman is a wonderful choice," AFL-CIO President John Sweeney said after her swearing-in.
Born in Mobile, Ala., Herman is a graduate of Xavier University and began her career in 1969 as a social worker for Catholic Charities.
That led to her service in a black women's employment project in Atlanta and her apppointment in 1977 as director of the National Minority Women's Employment Program.
Herman is single and has no children.
